name: Page Structure Rulebook
summary: Which pages a site needs, which sections a landing page has and in what order, and how pricing, contact and footers are built.
check: Compare the sitemap with `blueprints/site-types.md` and the section order with `blueprints/landing-page.md`.
Scroll the home page on a phone: the primary action is never more than one screen away.
Every price, quote, logo and number on the page has a source in `DECISIONS.md`.

sources.title: Baymard Institute: product page and checkout research
Orbit Media: website footer best practices

rules.title: Sitemap from the kind of site
rules.text: Start from the sitemap for the kind of site in `blueprints/site-types.md` and cut every page the business cannot fill with real content.

rules.title: Sections follow the visitor's questions
rules.text: Order the landing page as promise, proof, detail, objections, action: hero, proof strip, product or services, how it works, deep proof, pricing, FAQ, final CTA, footer (`blueprints/landing-page.md`).

rules.title: Leave out what cannot be filled
rules.text: A section without real content is removed, not faked with placeholders, stock quotes or invented numbers. Missing content goes on the list in `DECISIONS.md`.

rules.title: The offer is shown, not listed
rules.text: Services and features appear with real screenshots, photos, a demo or examples of the result, close to the top of the page.

rules.title: The primary action repeats
rules.text: The same primary action appears in the header, the hero, after the offer, after pricing and in the final CTA, and as a sticky bar on mobile once the hero button has scrolled away.

rules.title: Every page has a next step
rules.text: Inner pages (service, feature, case study, about) end with the primary action or a link to the page that closes the decision.

rules.title: Proof is specific and named
rules.text: Three to five testimonials with name, role and permission, client logos with permission, numbers with source and date. Fewer, specific proofs beat a long wall.

rules.title: Services that sell packages get tiers
rules.text: When a service is sold in packages, show three named packages built from the real offer, one recommended, same items in the same order, one action per card, add-ons and payment terms below (`blueprints/pricing.md`).

rules.title: Prices come from the business
rules.text: Use the real prices or "from" prices. When there are none yet, ask the user and mark placeholders in the build; never publish invented figures.

rules.title: A pricing page answers the rest
rules.text: Subscription and multi-tier products get a pricing page with a billing toggle that shows the saving, a comparison table grouped by category, an FAQ about payment and cancellation, and a route for custom needs.

rules.title: Comparison tables work on phones
rules.text: On small screens the comparison becomes an accordion per category or a tier switcher, with a sticky row of tier names; the page never scrolls sideways.

rules.title: Contact is easy to find
rules.text: A page or section labelled Contact, linked from the header and the footer, with phone, email, address and hours as real text, response time, and a short form (`blueprints/contact.md`).

rules.title: Company contacts by need
rules.text: Companies route contacts by what the visitor needs (sales, support, press, careers, locations), not by the org chart, and always keep one main number and email.

rules.title: Footer size matches the site
rules.text: Slim for one-page sites, standard for small businesses, fat with four to six labelled columns, contact, newsletter and a legal row for companies, SaaS and shops (`blueprints/footer.md`).

rules.title: Legal row in the footer
rules.text: Legal name, registration and VAT numbers where required, privacy, terms, cookie settings and the accessibility statement sit in the last row of the footer.

rules.title: Features before the promise
rules.text: A features grid as the first thing under the header, before the visitor knows what the product is and who it is for.

rules.title: Hidden prices for simple offers
rules.text: "Contact us for pricing" on a small-business service or a self-serve product. Keep "contact us" for genuinely custom or enterprise work, and give a starting price when possible.

rules.title: Metal-named tiers
rules.text: Bronze, Silver, Gold, Platinum. Name tiers after the customer or the size of the job.

rules.title: More than one recommended plan
rules.text: Two highlighted cards, or a badge on every card. Recommend one.

rules.title: Contact only through a form
rules.text: A form as the only way to reach a business, or contact details hidden under About.

rules.title: Footer as a link dump
rules.text: Dozens of unsorted links, keyword lists, tag clouds or a copy of the header with nothing else.

rules.title: Every section a different layout trick
rules.text: A new effect, layout and component style in each section. One signature moment per page, the rest calm and consistent.

rules.title: Footer groups by what people look for
rules.text: Group footer links by job: product, company (about, careers, press), resources (help, status, blog), trust (security, compliance), legal. The last row carries ©, privacy, terms, cookie settings and the security contact. Size the footer to the site (`PG-14`); a small site needs only the legal row and contact.

rules.title: The cart is a drawer that sells
rules.text: Adding to the cart opens a cart drawer from the side (a bottom sheet on phones) instead of leaving the page. Top to bottom: the items with variant, quantity and remove; a progress line toward the next free gift or free shipping; two to four products that go with the cart; then a fixed footer with the total and one solid checkout button that never scrolls away. It closes with Escape, the close button or a click outside, and traps focus while open (`AX`). Full layout: `blueprints/cart.md`.

rules.title: A free-gift ladder instead of discount codes
rules.text: To raise the order value, show tiers of free gifts at the next spend thresholds, spaced about 50–100 USD (1 000–2 000 Kč) apart and starting just above the current average order. Pick gifts that cost little to make, weigh little to ship and look valuable (a cap, socks, a tote, a sample size). Show the next step in words ("Add 450 Kč for a free cap") and a gift that is reached appears in the cart as a line priced "Free". Fashion brands report that gifts move order value and conversion more than a discounted checkout or free shipping; still measure it on your shop.

rules.title: One-click add-ons that need no choice
rules.text: Products suggested in the cart are complementary and one size (a cap, a bracelet, socks, care products), so a single click adds them without opening a size picker. Show two to four, each with image, name and price, plus an add button. Measure revenue per visitor. When the cart is empty or holds one item, recently viewed products are a good second row.

rules.title: A paid extra hidden in the checkout button
rules.text: Never put a paid extra (shipping protection, order insurance, free-returns plans, donations) into the price of the main checkout button and leave the cheaper path as a weaker secondary button such as "Continue without free returns". It is a pre-selected extra payment: banned in the EU by the Consumer Rights Directive (article 22 requires express consent, no default options) and treated by the US FTC as a hidden junk fee. Offer it as its own clearly priced switch above the button, off by default, and keep the checkout button showing the real total of what the person chose.

rules.title: Test cart changes on order value, not clicks
rules.text: Every cart change (gift tiers, add-ons, button order, copy) ships as an A/B test with a holdout, judged on average order value, conversion rate and revenue per visitor over at least two full weeks, and on returns and complaints after that. A change that only raises clicks is not a win.
